title: Searching for dark matter with the purest materials on Earth
excerpt: Using bubbles, crystals, prehistoric rocks, and more, scientists look for signals from the invisible part of the universe
content:
Key Insights

  • On Sept. 1, 2026, researchers reported what may be the first ever detection of dark matter, a mysterious and invisible substance that makes up nearly 85% of all matter in the universe.
  • The success was thanks to countless chemists and physicists who make dark matter detectors out of ordinary materials—xenon, fluorocarbons, silicon crystals, and more—pushed to physical extremes.
  • A single observation isn’t enough to understand dark matter completely, so researchers will continue to refine the purity of the materials they use in detectors to maximize the likelihood of another observation.

We like to believe we can see the universe: planets, stars, and galaxies. Yet these celestial bodies are just isolated islands within a vast, invisible ocean. Hidden between the stuff we can see is an imperceptible substance that sculpts the universe on the largest scales. Scientists call it dark matter.

Thus far, this strange stuff has never been directly detected. At least that was true until earlier this month, when researchers at a conference in Japan reported their recent findings.

According to the research team, a few flashes of light were recorded deep underground in a large vat of ultrapure liquid xenon. Even after months of analysis, the researchers could not find anything ordinary to explain the event. Those flashes may be the first direct proof of dark matter’s existence.

At first blush, dark matter and other hidden secrets of the cosmos may seem to fall squarely in the domain of physics. In large part, they do. But at the heart of the world’s most advanced dark matter detectors lie materials that are prepared, purified, and customized through chemistry.

"I'm a chemist working amongst a bunch of physicists. I could never have imagined that my studies in chemistry would result in me being a vital member of physics collaborations searching for dark matter."

The material we see in every star, planet, and person is just a tiny fraction of what truly exists. Scientists propose that unseen dark matter makes up nearly 85% of all matter. Researchers deduced its existence in the 1930s from astronomy observations that seemed to defy explanation.

“We first encountered dark matter while watching galaxies move within clusters,” says Benjamin Lehmann, a physicist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, referring to those studies.

Galaxy clusters are cosmic neighborhoods of galaxies that move toward each other under the pull of gravity. When astronomers measured the speeds of galaxies within these clusters and calculated the mass required to cause those speeds, the results were baffling. The quantity of visible matter fell far short. The best explanation, at the time, was that something unseen and heavy fills these clusters, causing a powerful gravitational pull. Nearly a century later, it’s still the best explanation.

This invisible matter explains why light bends around galaxies and why galaxies spin impossibly fast. Mounting evidence, albeit indirect, has made dark matter central to astrophysics.

Despite its cosmic influence, dark matter remains mysterious. No one has seen it interact with ordinary matter, making it almost impossible to study. Gravity values deduced from astronomy observations tell researchers about dark matter’s mass, not its nature or behavior, leaving much of the universe unknown.

The search for dark matter: Make it, break it, shake it

To hunt for dark matter, physicists use three main strategies: “We can make it, break it, or shake it,” Lehmann says. Particle colliders try to make dark matter by smashing ordinary matter together at high energies. Space telescopes look for signs of dark matter breaking apart, like γ rays and other radiation emanating through the universe from dark matter particle collisions in the galaxy. And to shake it, scientists around the world have built intricate instruments that push earthly matter to extremes, where dark matter might interact with the ordinary type and teach us something about the composition of dark matter.

"[Gravity] is so weak that I, a puny human, am fighting and winning against the gravity of the entire planet simply by picking up my phone."

Lehmann explains that observing dark matter interacting with regular matter is hard for two reasons. For one thing, dark matter is abundant throughout the universe, but it’s rare on Earth. “All of Earth’s dark matter would equal roughly the mass of a squirrel,” Lehmann says.

Furthermore, as far as researchers understand today, dark matter interacts only through gravity, the weakest force. “It is so weak that I, a puny human, am fighting and winning against the gravity of the entire planet simply by picking up my phone,” Lehmann says. This weakness means that the gravitational pull of a single particle of dark matter is infinitesimal, and there’s too little of the pull to add up to something that can be observed through gravity.

The best chance for detecting dark matter on Earth relies on observing it interacting with ordinary matter in a way that does not depend on gravity. “This is very likely but rare,” Lehmann says. “We need a detector sensitive enough to catch rare, unique events from scarce particles,” he adds. And here’s where chemistry and advanced materials come into play.

Chemists make the purest materials on Earth

A major challenge to detecting dark matter is that some particles, like neutrons, can imitate the substance. These imposters can cause nuclear recoils in the detectors and generate misleading signals that look like dark matter. Sunlight, nuclear radiation, and cosmic rays all carry such imposters, so detectors must be shielded from all possible radiation sources.

The first defense against misleading signals is to build detectors deep underground to shield them from most cosmic and solar radiation. LZ was built in a gold mine in Lead, South Dakota, as were the dark matter detectors in Sudbury. And XENONnT sits under the Gran Sasso d’Italia mountain group. Even so, some radiation slips through the rock, and some emanates directly from the rock. So detectors are also wrapped in multiple layers of shielding, “like Russian [nesting] dolls,” says Isaac Arnquist, a chemist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL), who previously worked on the PICO experiment and currently works on SuperCDMS.

“We go to great efforts to build these detectors,” Arnquist says. “But sometimes, we detect radiation from the detector itself.” That’s because most materials contain trace amounts of radioactive uranium, thorium, and potassium. For these experiments to work, the radiation coming from detector materials must be reduced by more than a factor of a million compared with ordinary materials. Reaching that goal requires extraordinarily pure materials. “That’s where I specialize—in finding or growing those materials,” Arnquist says.

"The copper we produce at PNNL is the most radiopure material on the planet."

Achieving the purity needed for shielding materials often demands unusual measures because effective radiation shielding requires dense substances—and the denser the material, the harder it is to purify.

Lead is dense, so it works well to shield external radiation. But even after removing uranium and thorium, it retains radioactive lead-210. That radioactivity is why physicists seek out old lead, which has had time for the lead-210 to decay. “Researchers have looked for this ancient lead,” Arnquist says. “They search for these Spanish galleons, sunk in the Mediterranean, to procure the lead, used for ballast, from the bottom of these ships.”

Tungsten, even denser than lead, is excellent for shielding. To purify it, researchers convert the metal to tungsten hexafluoride, a gas at ordinary temperatures and pressures. Then they react the gas with hydrogen, which re-forms metallic tungsten and leaves any impurities behind. Using this method, PNNL researchers have produced the purest tungsten ever made.

“The closer you get to the detector’s center,” which is usually copper or titanium, “the purer the materials must be,” Arnquist says. “The copper we produce at PNNL is the most radiopure material on the planet.” It’s created by dissolving copper in acid and then using electricity to separate pure copper from contaminants—a process far cleaner than melting and casting. This is the copper that is used in the casings and cables at the SuperCDMS crystal detector experiment.

"Dark matter experiments are a great example of classical separation chemistry, pushed to an extreme scale and purity requirement by fundamental physics."

LZ, meanwhile, uses a titanium tank for its xenon-filled cryostat. Minfang Yeh, a chemist at Brookhaven National Laboratory, says LZ scientists screened many samples of titanium before finding ultrapure material. “Two pieces of nominally similar commercial titanium can have dramatically different radioactivity depending on the ore, processing route, furnace history, and surface contamination,” Yeh says.

Verifying that materials used in detectors won’t eventually generate unwanted radiation calls for radioassaying the materials. Arnquist’s team uses a mass spectrometer to count radioactive atoms directly. “It’s like testing fish for mercury or paint for lead, except our mass spectrometers are on steroids, and they detect the smallest amounts of uranium, thorium, and potassium,” Arnquist says. “We work in cleanrooms, fully covered, to protect samples from our own radiation,” he says, finding irony in how it’s usually people who need shielding from samples and not the other way around.

Every part of the detectors—support structures, tiny screws, electronic connectors, and cables—must be radioassayed. Sometimes Arnquist’s team can source ultrapure materials from vendors. Other times they must purify materials themselves, reducing radioactive elements to part-per-trillion levels. This purification is especially important for the liquid xenon and the crystals at the center of the detectors.

Commercial xenon contains radioactive krypton-85. LZ researchers remove the impurity by flowing the xenon through a large chromatography column packed with an adsorbent. Because of their differing affinities for the adsorbent, xenon and krypton flow through the column at different rates and are collected separately. The challenge, Yeh says, is applying the process to tons of xenon while removing only trace amounts of krypton. “This is a great example of classical separation chemistry, pushed to an extreme scale and purity requirement by fundamental physics.”

Signals that look like dark matter

Despite researchers’ best efforts to eliminate false positives, a small number of neutrons, α particles, and other dark matter impostors still make it through the lines of defense and generate misleading signals. So scientists have devised additional means to reject these interfering signals that masquerade as dark matter interactions. Some of these methods depend heavily on chemistry.

One such example is the gadolinium-based liquid scintillator at the LZ detector. This device relies on the lanthanide’s knack for capturing stray neutrons. The snagged neutrons trigger a cascade of γ rays, which makes the scintillator flash and gives researchers a sign to discard the false positive.

But there’s a hitch. Gadolinium salts do not readily dissolve in the nonpolar organic liquids used in scintillators. As Yeh explains, researchers bypass that problem by using 3,5,5-trimethylhexanoic acid to turn gadolinium into an organosoluble carboxylate complex that remains stable in various organic solvents.

Neutrinos, nearly massless particles streaming from the sun and other radiation sources, also cause unwanted false signals and are harder to filter out than neutrons. Ironically, further increasing detector sensitivity to better detect dark matter will lead to more and more false positives from interfering neutrinos. Eventually, there will be no way to statistically distinguish the two signals. Physicists call this experimental confusion “neutrino fog.” Because of the high performance of today’s detectors, Lehmann says, many experiments are close to reaching this point. And reaching it would mean the end of all large-scale dark matter collaborations that rely on detecting nuclear recoils.

But the fog won’t end the search. Researchers have already been looking for new ways, besides nuclear collisions in dense materials, to detect dark matter. One approach is known as the Dark Matter Radio (DM Radio): an instrument that detects dark matter waves similar to how a radio picks up AM and FM signals. Another mature experimental program is based on analyzing ancient rocks for signs of dark matter.

Deep underground, Earth’s oldest rocks may have tracked dark matter for millions of years, with passing particles leaving microscopic damage. Researchers dig up these ancient minerals and then scan the materials slice by slice with powerful microscopes, searching for these telltale tracks.

Regardless of the search method, ultrapure, exotic materials are needed for dark matter experiments, Lehmann says. The chemists’ role here is just as important as the physicists’, Yeh adds.

Have we finally found dark matter?

Even after 4 decades of searching, scientists have never directly detected dark matter. But earlier this month, the search produced one of its most intriguing results so far. LZ recorded a particle interaction that just might have come from dark matter. The researchers spent months checking and rechecking the data, searching for ways to dismiss the signal as background noise, but the event survived all the checks. "We are very excited about the new results," Yeh says.

"Rare-event experiments are essentially ultra-trace analytical chemistry laboratories built at the scale of particle-physics experiments."

But, Yeh explains, it is still impossible to say whether this signal will prove genuine. It could be the result of a particle interaction that remains unknown to scientists. “With only one event, we cannot claim that we have detected dark matter yet.”

Even if the LZ data survive additional analyses, the search for dark matter is far from over. “We have spent the last 300 years or so trying to describe in quantitative language what the universe is made of,” Lehmann says. “And then suddenly we find out that we’re only describing 20% of the universe.”

The cosmic mystery of the other 80% drives researchers to find out what that strange stuff is, what it does, and what it is made of. So the search for extraordinarily rare interactions here on Earth continues.

“These rare-event experiments are essentially ultra-trace analytical chemistry laboratories built at the scale of particle-physics experiments,” Yeh says.

Arnquist shares that view. "I’m a chemist working amongst a bunch of physicists. I could never have imagined that my studies in chemistry would result in me being a vital member of physics collaborations searching for dark matter."
